result:
The proposed count looks right, but I did not verify the argument in full.

The answer is the number of non-decreasing triples with 2 ≤ a₁ ≤ a₂ ≤ a₃ ≤ N, which is C(N+1, 3) = (N−1)N(N+1)/6. This holds exactly when distinct triples give non-isomorphic surfaces.

The topological argument has two pieces of evidence behind it:

- **Invariants:** The Milnor number μ and the Seifert structure of the link at infinity are diffeomorphism invariants, so algebraic isomorphism preserves them.
- **Small cases:** The sample coincidences of μ at N=5 are separated by their links, for example H₁ = ℤ/5 against (ℤ/2)².

The case analysis is only sketched. In the all-αᵢ=1 case the solution reports comparing the pairs (g, μ) across parameter families and finding no collisions, without showing that comparison. I also recall, without being able to confirm it, a published classification stating that affine Fermat-type varieties x₁^{a₁}+…+xₙ^{aₙ}+1 are isomorphic only when their exponent multisets agree. That matches the conclusion that all triples give distinct surfaces.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
